Buy and Sell Caution
Hamilton Police are reminding the public to exercise caution when buying and selling items through online marketplaces, following a recent robbery in the city.
On March 22, 2026, at approximately 9:30 p.m., police were called to a residence in east Hamilton for a reported robbery. A husband and wife had arranged the sale of an iPhone through Facebook Marketplace and agreed to meet the buyer at their home.
Upon arrival, the buyer was accompanied by two additional individuals. The couple observed that the group appeared uneasy. While one individual inspected the phone, the suspects suddenly fled the area on foot with the device. The husband pursued them, but the chase ended when he was sprayed with bear spray.
This incident marks the 14th marketplace-related robbery in Hamilton so far this year, with iPhones being the most commonly targeted item.
The Hamilton Police Service continues to investigate this incident and is urging residents to take precautions when conducting online transactions:
Meet in a public place:
Choose well-lit, busy locations. Hamilton Police Station 30 (400 Rymal Road East) offers a designated “Buy and Sell Zone” for safe transactions.
Check profiles carefully:
Be cautious of newly created accounts with little or no history, personal details, or transaction reviews.
Bring someone with you:
Attend meetups with a friend or inform someone of your meeting location and expected time.
Use secure payment methods:
Whenever possible, use electronic money transfers. Police have also seen incidents involving counterfeit cash.
Trust your instincts:
If something feels unsafe or suspicious, leave the situation immediately. There will always be other opportunities to buy or sell.

title: Hamilton Police Warn About Fentanyl Gummies
content:
NewsRelease_SEP06_2024
Hamilton Police are issuing a warning after fentanyl-laced gummies were found during a recent warrant.
These dangerous substances, disguised as candy, pose a serious risk to public health and safety, particularly for youth who may unknowingly consume them.
What to Know:
Fentanyl is a powerful opioid, up to 100 times stronger than morphine, and even a small amount can cause a fatal overdose.
The fentanyl-laced gummies resemble regular candy, making them particularly dangerous for children and teens, as well as unsuspecting adults.
The gummies are often brightly colored and packaged in ways that could easily be mistaken for legitimate, store-bought products.
Warning Signs of Fentanyl Exposure:
Drowsiness or unresponsiveness
Difficulty breathing
Confusion or dizziness
Slow or weak pulse
If you or someone you know displays any of these symptoms after consuming a product resembling gummies or candy, call 911 immediately. Time is critical in preventing a potential overdose.
Hamilton Police urge parents, caregivers, and teachers to be vigilant and speak with children and young adults about the dangers of ingesting unknown substances.
What You Can Do:
Avoid accepting any candy or edibles from unknown sources.
Monitor what your children bring home, especially if they have been at parties or events.
Share this warning with friends and family to raise awareness.
Fentanyl is highly potent and unpredictable. Even a small amount can be deadly.

title: Project Odeon Dismantles Significant Illegal Opioid Producers
content:
Hamilton Police Service along with the Ontario Provincial Police, York Regional Police, Toronto Police Service and several other law enforcement agencies have dismantled a significant producer of fentanyl and other synthetic drugs in the Greater Hamilton and Toronto Area (GTHA).
Project Odeon began after police discovered a clandestine laboratory during an overdose death investigation in November 2021 at a residence on Hamilton’s Mountain. Investigators subsequently suspected a link between this death, an earlier overdose resulting in hospitalization and a death at a Toronto condominium. These all occurred within days of each other.
Opioid addiction has resulted in significant and far-reaching impacts on Hamilton. Like many other communities across the GTHA, Hamilton has been grappling with the devastating consequences of the opioid epidemic and declared a state of emergency in April 2023 related to homelessness, opioid addiction and mental health.
“As police, we have witnessed firsthand the devastating impact of opioids. These substances have not only led to a surge in addictions and overdoses but have also strained our resources as we respond to calls for service. Through Project Odeon, we have made a significant dent in the production of opioids and we believe this will have an impact on public safety in our community,” says Superintendent Marty Schulenberg.
From January 1 to July 30, 2023, there have been 606 incidents related to suspected opioid overdoses and 89-suspected drug-related deaths in Hamilton. These numbers have been steadily rising over the past five years.
“We are encouraged by the outcome of many long hours of investigatory work and thank our law enforcement partners for their continued commitment to reducing the production and distribution of drugs in Hamilton. Ultimately, the seizure of these opioids contributes to reducing the harms associated with opioid use for those who use substances, their family and friends, and the broader community,” says Julie Prieto, Director, Hamilton Public Health Services Epidemiology and Wellness Division.
By tracing the origins of some of the lab equipment, investigators were able to identify a company in the United States. This business sold three items of laboratory equipment to an Oshawa-based company. From here, investigators were able to piece together an extended drug network.
Warrants were executed in Hamilton, Mount Albert, Smithville, Toronto, Whitchurch-Stouffville, and Vaughan.
In total, investigators seized the following items:
An operational fentanyl drug lab at 6800 Sixteen Road, Smithville.
A dismantled fentanyl drug lab at 4057 Bethesda Road, Stouffville.
Approximately 3.5 tons of chemical byproduct from fentanyl production.
800 gallons of chemicals commonly used in the production of fentanyl
Lab equipment commonly used in the production of fentanyl
64.1 kg of illicit drugs, including 25.6 kg of fentanyl, 18 kg methamphetamine, 6 kg of ketamine
A loaded, Glock firearm and ammunition and four extended magazines
Over $350,000 of seized proceeds, including cars, jewelry, furniture and cash

title: Hamilton Police Address Increase in Youth Violence
content:
Launch of Project Breathe Easy
Bear Spray - Info session
Hamilton Police Service is advising the community of a concerning increase in youth-related violent incidents, including a rise in the misuse of bear spray during altercations.
Over the past several months, officers have responded to a number of incidents involving young persons engaged in assaults, group conflicts, and weapons-related offences. Of particular concern is the growing trend of youth carrying and deploying bear spray in disputes.
Since March 3, police have responded to five incidents, with three youths facing charges.
Bear spray-related incidents have steadily increased each year between 2021 and 2025, representing a 115 per cent rise over the past five years. Youth aged 10 to 19 account for approximately 63 per cent of identified offenders. The most frequently reported offence involving bear spray is assault with a weapon.
Bear spray is designed as a wildlife deterrent and contains a highly concentrated irritant. When discharged in public spaces such as schools, malls, transit, or residential areas, it can cause significant respiratory distress, temporary blindness, panic, and serious safety risks to bystanders. When used against another person, bear spray is considered a weapon under the Criminal Code and may result in criminal charges.
While most youth in Hamilton make positive choices and contribute meaningfully to our community, the recent increase in violence highlights the need for proactive education, prevention, and enforcement.
In response to this trend, Hamilton Police have launched Project Breathe Easy, a targeted initiative aimed at reducing bear spray-related violence in the community.
Project Breathe Easy includes increased enforcement and high-visibility patrols in identified hotspot areas, proactive engagement with youth, compliance checks at retailers selling bear spray to ensure adherence to applicable legislation and responsible sales practices and ongoing monitoring and intelligence-led response to emerging concerns. The initiative combines enforcement with education to address both access and misuse.
“We don’t see a lot of bears walking around Hamilton. The reality is, we don’t have a bear problem — we have a youth safety problem that needs to be addressed,” says Chief Frank Bergen. “We’re not here to alarm families — we’re here to support them. At the same time, we are taking enforcement action where necessary to keep our community safe.”
Community Information Sessions
In addition to enforcement efforts, Hamilton Police are hosting a series of community information sessions aimed at parents and caregivers.
The sessions will focus on:
Current youth violence trends
The risks and legal implications of bear spray misuse
Warning signs parents should be aware of
How social media contributes to conflict escalation
Strategies for prevention and early intervention
Available community and mental health resources
Both in-person and virtual sessions will be offered to ensure accessibility for families across Hamilton. The virtual session will include breakout rooms in Arabic, Urdu, and French to support inclusive community dialogue.

from 5:30 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. at Central Library, 55 York Blvd, Hamilton

Hamilton Police emphasize that youth violence prevention requires collaboration between families, schools, community organizations, retailers, and law enforcement.
Early conversations at home, awareness of peer dynamics and online activity, and engagement in positive activities are among the strongest protective factors for young people.
“These sessions are about education, prevention, and accountability,” adds Inspector Frank Miscione. “We want parents to feel informed and supported, and we want youth to understand there are real consequences when weapons are brought into conflicts.”
Members of the community are encouraged to attend and participate in the discussions.

Hamilton Police have arrested a 28-year-old Mississauga man after officers responding to a suspicious vehicle call located a stolen vehicle and recovered a loaded firearm on Hamilton’s west mountain.

During a search of the vehicle, officers located a loaded Glock handgun on the front passenger seat. The accused has been identified as 28-year-old Sammy Shaik of Mississauga. He has been charged with:

title: Missing Hamilton Man Marcin Sydor Found Deceased; Death Ruled Homicide
content:
NewsRelease_JUNE01-2026
Hamilton Police are investigating the homicide of 48-year-old Marcin SYDOR after his body was located on Friday, May 29, 2026, in the area of Pier 16 near 386 Wilcox Street.
At approximately 8:00 a.m., Hamilton Police responded after receiving a report that a body had been located along the shoreline.
Officers attended and secured the area. With the assistance of the Hamilton Police Marine Unit, the body was recovered. Hamilton Police Forensic Services attended to process the scene.
The body was transported for a post-mortem examination, which has since been completed. The deceased was positively identified as Marcin SYDOR, a 48-year-old Hamilton man who had been reported missing to Hamilton Police on April 27, 2026.
The post-mortem examination determined that Marcin's death was the result of a homicide. The cause of death and details surrounding his injuries are not being released at this time in order to protect the integrity of the ongoing investigation.
Marcin's disappearance prompted an extensive missing person investigation. Investigators pursued numerous avenues in an effort to locate him after his absence was reported and quickly determined that his disappearance was out of character and inconsistent with his usual behaviour.
What began as a missing person investigation has now become a homicide investigation.
Hamilton Police extend condolences to Marcin's family and loved ones.
The Homicide Unit has assumed carriage of the investigation and is working to determine the circumstances surrounding Marcin's death and identify those responsible.
Investigators are asking anyone who had contact with Marcin, observed him, or has information regarding his activities and movements prior to his death to contact police. Investigators are also seeking information regarding Marcin's black 2014 Volkswagen Jetta with tinted windows.

title: Two Youths Charged in Counterfeit Currency Investigation
content:
The Hamilton Police Service Financial Crimes Unit has concluded a significant investigation into a series of frauds involving counterfeit currency used in Facebook Marketplace transactions.
In December 2025, investigators began examining multiple reports from victims who had sold items through Facebook Marketplace and were subsequently paid with counterfeit Canadian currency. In each incident, the suspects used fictitious Facebook accounts to arrange meetings with sellers at locations in Hamilton’s west end. During these transactions, the suspects provided counterfeit bank notes in exchange for merchandise, leaving victims unaware that the currency was fraudulent until after the sale.
Investigators believe more than 10 incidents are linked to the same suspects. To date, victims have received in excess of $20,000 in counterfeit currency.
As a result of the investigation and the execution of several search warrants, two male youths, aged 15 and 14, were arrested and charged.

Fraud Under $5,000 (3 counts)

Possession of Property Obtained by Crime (3 counts)
14-year-old male youth charged with:
Fraud Under $5,000 (3 counts)

Meet in a public, well-lit location.

title: Hamilton Police Downtown Substation Opens
content:
IMG_1363
Hamilton Police opened its new downtown substation at
2 King Street West (Jackson Square), creating a dedicated police presence in the heart of the city’s downtown core.
The new substation responds directly to concerns raised by downtown businesses, residents, service providers and community partners about safety, visibility and the need for stronger connections in the core.
Last month, Hamilton Police hosted a
Downtown Safety Summit, bringing together a broad cross-section of downtown partners to discuss the challenges facing the area and identify practical steps to support a safer, more vibrant and welcoming downtown. “We heard clearly from businesses and residents that a stronger police presence downtown matters,” said Chief Bergen. “This substation puts our officers closer to the people we serve, increases visibility, and strengthens our work with partners to keep downtown Hamilton safe, welcoming and vibrant.”
The 3504 square foot substation will be staffed using current Hamilton Police resources and will support the ongoing work of CORE Patrol and other members assigned to downtown safety initiatives.
“We are not alone in wanting people to feel safer moving throughout the downtown core. The Downtown Safety Summit demonstrated a real collective energy for positive change by the City, businesses and community partners,” said Bergen.
The new substation will be open from Monday to Saturday, 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. The City of Hamilton is leasing the space for $1 per year over the next two years from Jackson Square.

title: Hamilton Police Release 2025 Use of Force Data
content:
Numbers show a 28 per cent decrease over 2024
Hamilton Police Service has released its
2025 Use of Force Report, providing the public with information about when force was used, the circumstances surrounding those incidents, and the work underway to strengthen transparency, accountability and community trust.
While use of force by police officers is rare, there are situations where it may be necessary to protect members of the public, officers and the broader community. At the same time, Hamilton Police recognizes that every use-of-force incident can have a significant impact on the individuals involved, their families, communities and public trust.
In 2025, Hamilton Police recorded 203 use-of-force incidents involving individuals. This represents a 28 per cent decrease from 2024 and the lowest number of person-involved use-of-force incidents recorded during the six-year reporting period. These incidents involved 323 individuals, down from 452 in 2024.
The Use of Force report is intended to provide more than statistics. It supports informed public dialogue about how often force is used, the circumstances in which it occurs, how incidents are reviewed and how the Service continues to learn from the data.
“Use-of-force numbers are important, but they do not tell the whole story,” said Chief Frank Bergen. “Every incident involves people, and we recognize the impact these interactions can have on individuals, families and communities. Releasing this information publicly is one way we continue to invite informed discussion with the community.”
The 2025 report shows that use-of-force incidents remained concentrated in higher-risk circumstances. Weapon-related incidents and warrant executions accounted for nearly half of all person-involved use-of-force incidents. Approximately 75 per cent of incidents involved a subject who was perceived to have access to a weapon at the time of the interaction.
Firearm discharges involving individuals remained rare, with one firearm discharge recorded in 2025. Firearm pointing also declined to its lowest level in the six-year reporting period.
This year’s report includes additional analysis of recovered weapons and objects to provide greater transparency around incidents where officers perceived a firearm or edged weapon. This analysis helps distinguish between incidents involving confirmed weapons, imitation or replica firearms, gun-shaped objects, intelligence-led operations, and incidents where officers were responding to reports, behaviour, or investigative information indicating a possible weapon-related risk.
Hamilton Police continues to meet mandated training requirements for new recruits and serving police officers for use of force and mental health crisis response. The Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion strategy complements legislative training with experiential learning aimed at increasing cultural and identity competencies as well as reducing biases.
The report also includes available demographic information, including perceived gender, age and race. These findings are descriptive and must be interpreted carefully. Counts alone do not explain why differences may exist, whether disparities persist in similar circumstances, or how racialized communities experience these interactions.
Hamilton Police continues to examine these questions through its
Race and Identity-Based Data Strategy, in collaboration with the Community Advisory Panel. This work brings together data, community priorities and lived experience to better understand disparity, context and community impact.
Since June 2024, members of the Community Advisory Panel have met regularly with Hamilton Police and independently to review research, discuss analytical approaches, participate in use-of-force training, support community engagement and develop recommendations to strengthen transparency, accountability and equity in policing. The CAP recently presented
recommendations
on the RIBD Strategy.
On June 15, 2026, Hamilton Police has also hosted a community information session on use-of-force reporting, officer training, legal frameworks and local data. This session provided an opportunity for residents to ask questions, raise concerns and share their perspectives.
“Transparency is not only about releasing data,” said Chief Bergen. “It is about creating space for the community to understand the information, ask questions, raise concerns and help shape how we improve.”
While use-of-force remained rare relative to overall police-public contact in 2025, occurring in approximately 0.10 per cent of interactions, Hamilton Police recognizes that each incident can have a significant impact on the individuals involved, their families, communities and public trust. The Service remains committed to public reporting, ongoing analysis, community engagement and continuous improvement in how use-of-force incidents are reviewed, understood and discussed with the public.

title: One Person Deceased Following Three-Vehicle Collision on Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway
content:
Hamilton Police are investigating a fatal three-vehicle collision on the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway that claimed the life of a 24-year-old woman.

A Hamilton Police investigation into organized retail theft has resulted in 32 people facing 235 criminal charges, the recovery of more than $300,000 in suspected stolen property, and the seizure of a 2021 Ram TRX valued at approximately $100,000.
After a 25 per cent increase in thefts at Hamilton Home Depot stores, Hamilton Police launched
Project Checkout
to identify those responsible and disrupt the organized resale of stolen merchandise.
What began as a series of shoplifting investigations quickly revealed an organized operation. Investigators found organized groups were stealing high-value tools and construction equipment from Hamilton Home Depot stores before reselling the items through online marketplaces at prices well below retail. In several incidents, offenders threatened violence when store employees attempted to intervene.
During the four-month investigation, police executed two search warrants at a commercial property and a residence, recovering hundreds of suspected stolen tools and other items believed to be connected to the theft ring. A 2021 Ram TRX, believed to be proceeds of crime and valued at approximately $100,000, was also seized.
Organized retail theft extends far beyond the store. Stolen property is often resold online, fuelling criminal activity while driving up costs for businesses and consumers. By disrupting this network, investigators recovered stolen property, prevented additional offences and removed a significant supply of stolen merchandise from the illegal marketplace.
Hamilton Police worked closely with Home Depot's Asset Protection Team, whose ongoing partnership and information sharing were instrumental in the success of the investigation.

title: Eight Impaired Drivers Removed from Hamilton Roads Over the Weekend
content:
Hamilton Police charged eight drivers with impaired driving-related offences over the weekend, highlighting the continued danger impaired driving poses to everyone on our roads.
The incidents occurred across the city and included traffic stops, motor vehicle collisions, reports from concerned members of the public, and information shared by a partner police service.
Among the incidents:
A driver was located after their vehicle ended up in a ditch. The caller, concerned the driver had been drinking, contacted police.
A driver failed to stop at an intersection, causing a collision that sent another motorist to hospital with minor injuries.
Officers located a driver unconscious behind the wheel of a running vehicle in the middle of the roadway after receiving a report from the public.
Drivers were stopped after officers observed dangerous driving behaviours, including excessive speed and an inability to maintain a lane.
One driver refused to comply with a lawful breath demand, which is a Criminal Code offence carrying the same serious consequences as impaired driving.
Several of the drivers provided breath samples registering well over twice the legal limit.
These eight arrests are a reminder that impaired driving remains a persistent public safety issue in our community. Every one of these incidents was preventable. In one weekend alone, impaired driving resulted in collisions, injuries, and dangerous situations that put innocent road users at risk.
Hamilton Police continue to rely on a combination of proactive enforcement and information from the public to identify and remove impaired drivers from our roads. We thank the community members who recognized the signs of impairment and contacted police. Their actions may have prevented serious injury or even saved a life.
Whether impairment is caused by alcohol, drugs, or a combination of both, the message is simple: if you're impaired, don't drive. Plan ahead, arrange a designated driver, use a taxi or rideshare service, take public transit, or stay where you are until you are sober.
If you suspect someone is driving while impaired, call 9-1-1 immediately. Your call could prevent the next collision and help keep Hamilton's roads safe.

content:
Hamilton Police recorded
332 hate/bias incidents, including 138 criminal offences in 2025
—a
12 per cent increase
from the previous year. While this rise is concerning, it continues to reflect growing community trust in reporting and strengthened officer training in identifying hate-motivated incidents.
The majority of occurrences were
racially motivated, followed by incidents involving
religion
and
sexual orientation
. The
Black
,
Jewish, and
2S&LGBTQIA+
communities were most frequently impacted. Hate-motivated graffiti accounted for
54 per cent of the 138 hate crimes reported in 2025, making it the most common type of hate crime.
This year's report
also reflects changes to how hate crimes are classified using a national framework developed by Statistics Canada. The updated system allows police to record more than one hate motivation and recognize when an incident targets multiple protected groups. These changes improve the accuracy and consistency of hate crime data and provide a better understanding of hate-motivated incidents in Hamilton.
“Hate crimes and hate incidents can have a lasting impact on victims and the communities they target,” said Chief Frank Bergen. “By reporting these incidents, supporting those affected and working together, we can build a safer, more inclusive Hamilton where hate is not tolerated.”
Despite the increase in reports, hate crimes remain
vastly underreported
. Hamilton Police continue to encourage all individuals to report hate/bias incidents, no matter how minor they may seem.
In June 2024, Hamilton Police launched the
Hate Crime Case Review Team (HCCRT)
—a collaborative, community-driven initiative to improve accountability and transparency in hate crime investigations.
The HCCRT is composed of
14 community representatives
from the 2S&LGBTQIA+, Black, Indigenous, Jewish, Muslim, and South Asian communities. Members were selected through an open application and community voting process, ensuring diverse and intersectional representation.
In 2025, the team reviewed 50 of a
randomized sample of 124 hate-related cases (2018–2021)
—a statistically significant 95 per cent confidence sample. Their insights will help shape service delivery, identify gaps, and strengthen Hamilton Police’s response to hate-motivated incidents. A final report with recommendations is expected in December 2026.
Since 2019, Hamilton Police have implemented proactive strategies to prevent and respond to hate crimes, including:
Conducted 13 community presentations to raise awareness about reporting
Hosted the Hate Crime Symposium at Carmen’s Event Centre, with 150 participants attending
Supported 111 new victims through HPS Victim Services in 2025.
Delivered mandatory hate crime training for all new recruits, cadets, special constables and victim service volunteers.
Continued education for front-line patrol officers and supervisors
Expanded
online reporting tools
Joined the OPP-led Provincial Anti-Terrorism Section (PATS) enhancing intelligence sharing, risk assessment
Hamilton Police remain committed to ensuring this city is safe, inclusive, and welcoming for everyone.
“Together, we can break the cycle of hate. It starts with listening, learning, and standing up for each other,”
said Chief Bergen.
Hate crimes and bias-motivated incidents can be reported in several ways. In an emergency, call 911. For non-emergencies, call 905-546-4925. Reports can also be made online at
www.hamiltonpolice.on.ca
or in person at any Hamilton Police Service station.
For those who wish to provide information anonymously, please consider reaching out to Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 or submit your anonymous tips online at
Crime Stoppers Hamilton's Website
.

Over $5,000
Failure to Comply

Order

title: Two Arrested in Molotov Cocktail and Stolen Auto Investigation
content:
Two males have been arrested, and a Molotov cocktail has been seized following an overnight investigation into a stolen vehicle.
On July 23, 2026, at approximately 11:55p.m., Hamilton Police were proactively patrolling the area of Upper Horning Road when a stolen black Honda Civic vehicle was spotted. A traffic stop was attempted; however, the vehicle attempted to flee, striking a marked Police cruiser in the process.
The two occupants exited the vehicle and fled on foot while officers gave chase. Both were taken into police custody and one of the males suffered an injury. As a result, the Special Investigation Unit (SIU) has invoked their mandate.
During a search of the vehicle, officers located a Molotov cocktail. The device was seized and the vehicle was towed for further examination.
A 17-year-old male youth from York and a 22-year-old male from Brampton will now go before the courts to face the following charges:
· Possession of Property Obtained by Crime over $5000.00
· Flight from Police Officer
· Possession of Incendiary Material
· Possession Contrary to Order
If anyone has information that they believe can assist Police with the investigation, please contact the on-duty Division 30 Staff Sergeant at 905-546-3886. To submit information anonymously, please contact Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477) or visit crimestoppershamilton.com

title: Hamilton Police Seeking Members for New 2SLGBTQIA+ Advisory Committee
content:

Hamilton Police Service is inviting community members to apply to join the Chief’s 2SLGBTQIA+ Advisory Committee.
The committee provides advice directly to the Chief of Police on issues affecting Hamilton’s 2SLGBTQIA+ communities. Members help identify community concerns, strengthen relationships, improve police services and support equitable and inclusive policing across Hamilton.
Hamilton Police is seeking applicants who are passionate about their community and committed to helping build a safer, more inclusive city.
Applications are encouraged from individuals who reflect the diversity and intersectionality of Hamilton’s communities, including Indigenous people, newcomers, members of different faiths, non-binary people, older adults, persons with disabilities and racialized individuals.

.

title: Female Arrested in Romance Scam
content:

money.

Unit launched an
investigation into an
alleged romance fraud

man.

met and developed
a relationship with

March

provide approximately $20,000 after claiming

assistance to cover

expenses,
assuring him the
money would be
repaid. Police allege
the funds
were obtained through
deception.

Police Service
Crimes Against Seniors
Unit arrested

Falls. She
has been charged
